extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, literary readers and critics, and writers interested in morals and poetic criticism (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_short: writing literary criticism and moral essays
extracted.subtask_description: Short, periodical essays giving moral reflections and literary criticism (early-18th-century Spectator-style) that evaluate behaviour, authorial responses to reproach, and poetic qualities in epic poetry such as Milton's Paradise Lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ostentatious devotion disparages true sanctity
rubrics_metrics.description: This ostentatious Behaviour is such an Offence to true Sanctity, that it disparages it, and makes Virtue not only unamiable, but also ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: public theatrical piety (carrying abridged morality to display, ostentatious prayers, covering the face at tea, ejaculations before supper). Biblical/sacred writings condemn such conduct; affectation of devotion deters others from goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypocritical devotion deters others from religion
rubrics_metrics.description: A Devotée is so far from promoting Goodness, that she deters others by her Example. Folly and Vanity in one of these Ladies, is like Vice in a Clergyman; it does not only debase him, but makes the inconsiderate Part of the World think the worse of Religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: avoid hypocrisy in religious display because it not only cheapens virtue but harms the perception of the whole institution; sincerity is required to promote social good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty of look and manners as sign of true courage
rubrics_metrics.description: There was so much Modesty in their Looks... This Virtue, which is always join'd to Magnanimity, had such an influence upon their Courage, that in Battel an Enemy could not look them in the Face, and they durst not but Die for their Country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Spartan modesty (Xenophon) is contrasted with London affectation; modest demeanour is presented as genuine courage, while loud bravado is mere show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affectation of smartness, wit, and courage is ridiculous
rubrics_metrics.description: These things arise from a general Affectation of Smartness, Wit, and Courage... from such Hints I beg a Speculation on this Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: red breeches as a 'certain Sign of Valour', tripping up a beggar to boast agility, mockery of country gentry. Affectation invites ridicule from the 'Polite Rabble.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to reproach: examine truth, then either reform or be indifferent
rubrics_metrics.description: Does a Man reproach thee for being Proud or Ill-natured... Consider with thy self whether his Reproaches are true; if they are not ... he reviles an Imaginary Being ... If his Reproaches are true ... become mild, affable and obliging, and his Reproaches of thee naturally cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epictetus' practical rule: when faced with criticism, first self-examine; if criticism is false, treat it as aimed at an imaginary portrait and do not be wounded; if true, correct conduct. This is framed as a piece of fortitude every person owes to their innocence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbearance and suppressing satirical replies is noble
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Man has any Talent in Writing, it shews a good Mind to forbear answering Calumnies and Reproaches in the same Spirit of Bitterness with which they are offered... to let drop his Wrath, and stifle his Resentments, seems to have something in it Great and Heroical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: authors should refrain from launching satirical or bitter public retaliations; the writer gains greater moral credit and personal satisfaction by suppressing lampoons and invectives (Boccalini's Traveller anecdote supports ignoring nuisances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making public works into personal polemics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Work would have been of very little use to the Publick, had it been filled with personal Reflections and Debates; for which Reason I have never once turned out of my way to observe those little Cavils which have been made against it by Envy or Ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for authors: do not fill publications with private quarrels or personal rejoinders; such material reduces public utility and distracts from the work's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of persons strengthens an epic's final book
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tenth Book of Paradise Lost has a greater variety of Persons in it than any other in the whole Poem... it is like the last Act of a well-written Tragedy, in which all who had a part in it are generally drawn up before the Audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical criterion for epic poetry: include and harmonize the multiple parties affected by the action in the dénouement to give the work completeness and tragic finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful and poetic incorporation of Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: The Author... has also kept religiously to the Form of Words, in which the three several Sentences were passed upon Adam, Eve, and the Serpent. He has rather chosen to neglect the Numerousness of his Verse, than to deviate from those Speeches which are recorded on this great occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: where Scripture is invoked or alluded to, preserve the weight and form of sacred speeches when it serves the poem; weave allusions into the poem poetically rather than forcing many citations for their own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sublime imagery and large imaginative incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Accordingly they are represented as infecting the Stars and Planets with malignant Influences, weakning the Light of the Sun, bringing down the Winter into the milder Regions of Nature... the following Lines, in which we see the Angels heaving up the Earth... is conceived with that sublime Imagination which was so peculiar to this great Author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for epic effect: bold, cosmic-scale incidents (turning Earth's poles, perverting nature) executed with sublime imagination increase the poem's grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty of diction, careful judgment, and finishing touches
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beauty of the Diction is very remarkable in this whole Episode... the great Judgment with which it was contrived... Milton never fails of improving his own hints, and bestowing the last finishing Touches to every Incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic standard: refined, apt language (diction) and well-judged editorial finishing enhance scenes; the poet should polish incidents to give them their last effective stroke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray human characters with tenderness to elicit pity and compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton has by this means filled a great part of his Poem with that kind of Writing which the French Criticks call the Tender... Adam and Eve... are likewise drawn with such Sentiments as do not only interest the Reader in their Afflictions, but raise in him the most melting Passions of Humanity and Commiseration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for tragic/heroic poetry: humanize protagonists (Adam's remorse, Eve's tears and supplication) so readers sympathize; present failings as frailties that invite compassion rather than mere blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegorical/imaginary persons work best in short, apt expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Such beautiful extended Allegories are certainly some of the finest Compositions of Genius: but, as, I have before observed, are not agreeable to the Nature of an Heroick Poem... Homer... makes use of other such Allegorical Persons, it is only in short Expressions... they may rather be looked upon as Poetical Phrases than Allegorical Descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: personifications (e.g., Flight, Fear, Victory) are effective as brief, apt images or phrases; avoid long sequences where allegorical figures engage in extended action within heroic epics.
